How do you start building your own home bar set? Start buying pieces to make a specific drink? Then keep growing it by learning to make more drinks? Or buying a set at once?

I recently moved, and gave away a good portion of my home-bar prior to moving; gifts to friends, and such. So, in my new home I'm taking these steps to rebuild my collection. First and foremost, if you don't already have one - I'd start with a basic set of bar tools, you can find some details here. Now, when it comes to ingredients, I'm just slowly building it back up - whenever I'm craving a particular drink, or style of drink; I grab what I need, and add it to my collection. This will definitely go for any liquors, liqueurs, cordials, non-perishable mixes, etc. Having what you need for a drink often includes fresh juices, or fruit garnishes. These items, being perishable, will be more of an 'as you need it,' addition to your collection. But, after a while, you'll have a collection to be proud of - and utilizing some of the recipes found here, you're bound to have a good time, and develop an ecclectic collection in no time!
Pretty sure you wont get a better answer then this. Very informative thanks.

No, don't buy a set. Get a book, like Seagram's Bar Tending Guide, which is full of traditional recipes for more drinks than you have ever heard of. Next look up the drinks and drink types you like and start your liquor and mixer purchases. Make your favorite drinks and identify what you like and what you don't like about them. This is how you can easily expand and educate your palate. The next step is to take that information and apply it, note the things you don't like and then go to a mixology bar or a liquor store during off hours and talk to the mixologist or the owner/orderer to find better alternatives for those items.

Build your bar organically and you will end up with spirits that work with drinks you will actually consume and enjoy.

Let me start you off, Tito's Vodka.

Regarding tools, I would say that most quality items don't come in sets. This is generally true, but all rules have exceptions and I haven't been shopping recently.

Regarding spirits/ingredients, I would keep it simple and plan around my top 5 (or less...or maybe more) drinks that I would want available. Then (akin /u/howtokillagod's advice) I would look up other drinks that I can make with existing ingredients. As the list grows, I would add items that I just needed one more ingredient to make. The primary reason for this is that many ingredients will at least face some degradation, if not entirely go bad, so I wouldn't want to buy things that I wouldn't use.

The preceding presumes that you're using the home bar for the drinks. If you're wanting to make a training station to build your repertoire for whatever reason, then I would begin with additional popular drinks on your list and add accordingly.

==================

TL;DR: Growing it

I personally have a few decent bartending sets for different settings. Granted, I don't use them for high volume bartending so I can't really speak on durability although most are probably made in China, but they're really just variations of themselves. A decent set of equipment at a culinary store should get the job done for a home setting though - I would just avoid cheap looking, gimmicky, as seen on tv or wrapped in a box sets. (Those slow pourers are trash, the bottle opener and wine-key are probably going to last about a month and will need to be replaced, and you'll need a decent muddler)
Buy stuff that you like and buy stuff your friends like; make sure you drink slower than you buy. Your bar will grow over time.

Start with the hooch, then glassware when you have guests, then tools when you have a party. You can drink any drink out of a solo cup if you don't have glassware, but you can't make thin drinks if you don't have the ingredients. Glassware is nice for specific drinks, like stemware for martinis or wine, or copper mugs for moscow mules, but not strictly necessary. Tools can almost always be improvised, with no exceptions coming to mind ATM.
As far as what booze: Whisk(e)y, vodka, gin, tequila, and rum(light and dark) are your bases, I'm sitting pretty light ATM. Liqueurs: triple sec, kahlua, soco (I don't consider it liquer), and Drambuie. Add to that both vermouths, both common bitters, and common mixers(Rose's sweetened lime juice, grenadine, sour mix, simple syrup(if you're lazy). Also fruit: oranges, lemons, limes, and accompanying juices; Maraschino cherries, grapefruit juice, etc.
As far as barware, a couple different types of pint and rocks glasses, stemware -wine, martini, and champ glasses. Then get the fancy stuff, copper mugs for moscow mules comes to mind as a recent purchase of mine. If you really want to get fancy, absinthe glasses and spoons, and a decanter if you really want to get fancy. Basic stuff like muddlers, stir rods, shakers should be built up as needed, but don't worry if you have to improvise the basics, there's a reason they're called the basic.
If you want to go full on fancy, there's an almost infinite number of liqueurs, aperitifs, fruit. cut glass and full on crystal glassware. Then you move on to the fancy schmancy molecular mixology shit, which, personally, I believe is shit.
Me, myself, I have the big five liquors, triple sec, kahlua, both vermouths, both bitters, lime juice, grenadine, rose's sour mix, and 'the flavor of the week' fifth -usually sweet tea vodka in the summer.
For glassware: rocks glasses(double size), shot glasses, pint glasses, and a set of copper mugs.
For barware: just swizzle sticks, a pour rod, and a bfk for fruit.
And I'm looking into getting a kegerator, but funds are low ATM.
Most commercial bars setup their speed rail as follows: Vodka, Gin, Rum, Tequila, and Whiskey. 90% of bar drinks are these plus 1 or 2 mixers. Buy cheap supplies or expensive; but buy what YOU like.
Buy the ingredients for a drink whenever you party, restock when it runs out. Pretty soon you'll have everything you need.

I've modded my fair share of communities over the years and have learned a lot about the role of being a mod. I figured I could share some of it with you guys. Here's some do's and dont's that will help you.

The Dont's

  1. Don't try to silence people who don't have the same views as you. It's wrong and people will eventually find out.

  2. Don't say "haha, I'm a mod and I get to do whatever I want to". It makes you look like a bad mod and person. And people will not respect you.

  3. Don't make arbitrary rules or something you decide to make up on the spot to ban someone because you don't like them. Follow the rules that are already outline by you or someone else.

  4. Don't make a post about you banning someone. Keep it between you and the user who was punished. People see it as bragging about your powers.

  5. Don't use foul or unnecessary language when making a post response (especially when giving someone a warning). You want to present yourself as an upstanding member of the community, not someone with a lack of vocabulary and nonprefessional.

  6. Don't involve yourself in flamewars. Remove the post(s) ,give the offending users a warning and leave it at that.

  7. If you make a rule change make it known to the users (and the other mods).

  8. Just use common sense. If you think what your about to do is wrong don't do it

  9. Be watchful over your community. That doesn't mean you have to jump in and take sides. The best are often those uninterrupted with so those involved are freer to be themselves.

  10. Unless it starts getting out of hand, be easy on mod actions. More times than not, circumstances will resolve themselves without your aid as a mod.

  11. Do not be petty. Do not use your mod powers just because you can. Have a valid reason backed by the rules before taking action.

  12. Remember you are human too. Sometimes there are going things that get your goat. Rather than jump on it and act, if there is the slightest doubt you are not being fair, sleep on it.

  13. When circumstances permit, be magnanimous. Be good to your people, not a shit ass. You want respect, earn it by showing respect to others.

  14. If someone is buttering you up, ask yourself why? What do they gain from it? You don't have to make a public statement about it. This is just for yourself.

  15. Remember that in order to have a discussion there must be a disagreement to have opposite sides. Disagreement is often a good thing.

9-15 provided by /u/BBQue

The Do's

  1. Help people as much as possible. It sticks with people when a mod helps them to the fullest.

  2. Be professional. This one's simple.

  3. Always strive to make the users happy and the community a good place.

  4. Respect people. Like the saying goes, "Respect is earned not given".

  5. Be a member of the community. Don't disappear then come back and act like nothing happened.

  6. Reward users who help others when you can't. We all like to be recognized for doing good.

And always remember, with power comes responsibility

I'm not suggesting that every sarcastic person lacks professional success, it was just an example to illustrate the point.

Where there is sarcasm there is frustration, a frustration about unfairness or about hopelessness, that is at the root of it. If it's not your job then it's some other important part of your life. Just as every cynic is a disillusioned idealist, every sarcastic comment is an ineffective cry against something that cannot be addressed directly. Sarcasm is clever and hostile, and expression of intelligence and ability and opposition. It's the substitute for the unreachable satisfaction of actually fixing the frustrating thing. It's a way of saying, well, I can't win here, but I can at least show you that I am smart and that I still oppose you. I have value, even if I cannot win.

Keep in mind that there are different sorts of weakness. Sometimes weakness is a refusal to fight, sometimes it's an inability to fight well, and sometimes it's all about fighting the wrong things. Everyone is weak if they try to fight against the tide. Sometimes people fight the tide because they think the tide was the problem, instead of the thing they should be fighting instead.

There is no such thing as a hopeless, inescapable fight. There are fights that you can win or escape, and there is fate. If you don't see it that way, then you are fighting against the tide somewhere.
